summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would change the large-scale renewable energy target yearly through to 2030.
It would let regulations provide full exemptions from the renewable energy target for electricity used in certain energy-intensive trade-exposed activities.
Native forest wood waste would be made eligible again as a renewable energy source, matching the rules before it was disallowed in 2011.
changes: Amends the annual renewable electricity targets under the large-scale Renewable Energy Target scheme each year until 2030.
Gives regulations power to grant full exemptions from the renewable energy target for electricity used in energy-intensive trade-exposed activities.
Removes the requirement for periodic reviews of the Act.
Reinstates native forest wood waste as an eligible renewable energy source under the same conditions as before its 2011 removal.
summary.affected: Electricity generators, businesses in energy-intensive trade-exposed industries, and operators using native forest wood waste for renewable energy.

Larissa Waters I thank the chamber for its indulgence; I believe now is the correct time to move under standing order 115(2) for a brief but necessary inquiry into this bill, the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015. It is highly unusual for us to not have inquiries into bills, particularly controversial bills like this one, which changes the face of our clean energy future. I am urging the chamber: whatever your position is on this bill—and we know that—unfortunately—both of the big parties are agreeing to cut the clean energy target—it is just abominable that you would do so without actually sending this bill to an inquiry. There is a litany of unanswered questions about the implications of this bill, not least about the native forest burning that has been included in the face of all evidence. The community deserves the right to have a say. That is the normal process. I am incredulous that we have already moved twice for an inquiry and have received no support. We are giving folk one last chance tonight. We are not trying to delay the passage of this bill. We understand that you guys want to slash the renewable energy target and we do not; we know we have lost that fight. But we do want to make sure that we actually scrutinise this bill, and so I move: That the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, together with the circulated amendments to the bill, be referred to the Environment and Communications Legislation Committee for inquiry and report by 22 June 2015. Stephen Parry The question is that the bill be referred to a committee on the motion moved by Senator Waters.

Janet Rice In speaking to our amendment regarding the removal of the ability to burn wood from native forests to be eligible for renewable energy certificates, the issue of what is classified as waste is pertinent and is behind our amendment. Minister Hunt has claimed repeatedly the biomass that is going to be burnt in forest furnaces is just waste, so we are interested in knowing exactly what is the government's definition of 'waste' or 'residue' in relation to the burning of native forest biomass for electricity. As far as we can see, nothing about this proposal to be burning wood from native forests for energy is about waste. Rather, it is about maintaining, entrenching and expanding industrial scale clear-fell logging that would not otherwise have occurred. It is not about branches, bark and treetops, as we have been misled to believe over the last months. If it were it would be restricted to this and would not include whole logs. In contrast, this legislation is all about allowing the burning of whole logs from native forests for electricity—it is so far from being renewable it is not funny. The statistics on logging in native forests show that in Victoria and New South Wales 70 to 80 per cent of the logs that are coming out of our clear-felled native forests are ending up as pulp logs; they are not being used as sawn timber. In Tasmania, 80 to 90 per cent of the logs are being classed as residual or pulp logs, not as saw logs. Under this legislation all of these logs will be able to be classified as waste. The higher values test would not stop this occurring as you would only have to get a very small amount of revenue from the use of the sawn timber. speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: The bill adjusts the large-scale renewable energy target to 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, aiming for 23.5% of electricity from renewables, increases exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries to full exemptions, reinstates native forest wood waste as an eligible renewable source, and removes biennial reviews of the target.

speeches.speaker: Mark Butler
speeches.brief: The opposition supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 except for part 4, arguing the bill stabilised the renewable energy industry after a "reckless" attack by the Prime Minister, which broke election promises made during negotiations between Minister Wong and then-shadow minister MacFarlane.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, which sets a Large-scale Renewable Energy Target of 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, resulting in over 23.5% of Australia’s electricity from renewable sources. The bill reduces the target from 41,000 gigawatt hours, reinstates biomass from native forest wood waste as eligible renewable energy, and provides full exemptions from RET costs for emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries like Tomago Aluminium.

speeches.speaker: Sharon Bird
speeches.brief: The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 reduces the large-scale renewable energy target to 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, extends full exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed activities, removes periodic reviews, and reinstates native wood waste as an eligible resource; the speaker supported the bill but opposed including native wood waste, arguing Labor will use the target as a floor to build a more ambitious post-2020 policy.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Broad
speeches.brief: The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 reduces the renewable energy target from 41,000 to 33,000 gigawatt hours, justified by changed energy use behaviour, industry moving offshore due to higher power prices, and improvements in solar and fossil fuel technology.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Nikolic
speeches.brief: The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 reflects a bipartisan agreement between the government and opposition on renewable energy targets.

speeches.speaker: Gai Brodtmann
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, which sets the large-scale renewable energy target at 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, projecting $40.4 billion in investment and 15,000 jobs, but opposed the reinstatement of native wood-waste biomass as an eligible renewable source, vowing to move an amendment to exclude it.

speeches.speaker: Jim Chalmers
speeches.brief: The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 rescales the renewable energy target from 41,000 to 33,000 gigawatt hours, provides assistance to emissions-intensive trade exposed industries, and includes wood waste. The speaker supported the first two elements but opposed the inclusion of wood waste.

speeches.speaker: George Christensen
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that renewable energy exists only through subsidies and welfare, and supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity Amendment) Bill 2015, which reduces the large-scale renewable energy target to 33,000 gigawatt-hours by 2020, grants full exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries, and reinstates biomass from native forest wood waste as eligible. The speaker also cited the Warburton review's cost estimates and noted the benefit for Sun Metals, a zinc refinery in their electorate.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The bill reduces the renewable energy target from 41,000 to 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, increases exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries, reinstates native forest wood waste as eligible biomass, and removes biennial reviews. The speaker argued the changes are necessary to prevent penalty payments, industry closures, and to address market distortions from previous Labor government policies that created “phantom credits.”

speeches.speaker: Pat Conroy
speeches.brief: The speaker argued in support of the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, stating it ends endless reviews and grants full exemptions to emissions-intensive trade-exposed industries. He criticised the coalition for causing an 88% fall in clean energy investment and 21,000 jobs at risk, and claimed Labor's compromise would deliver $10 billion in additional investment and 6,500 jobs.

speeches.speaker: Keith Pitt
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, arguing it would raise electricity costs for low-income households, waste billions in subsidies, and fail to deliver reliable renewable energy by 2020. He cited a median weekly income of $411 in his electorate, an 87% rise in electricity disconnections to 12,454 households, and cost comparisons of $36 per megawatt hour for coal versus $190 for solar and $120 for wind.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 would lock in $20 billion of malinvestment in 2,000 additional wind turbines, despite electricity demand being 20% lower than forecast and the market already oversupplied. The speaker argued that the bill would increase electricity costs, destroy wealth, and that wind turbines are not cost-effective without subsidies, citing a Grattan Institute report finding solar subsidies cost $9 billion more than benefits.

speeches.speaker: Gary Gray
speeches.brief: The Labor Party supports the revised Renewable Energy Target of 33,000 gigawatt hours but opposes the inclusion of native wood waste and calls for fixing the self-generation exemption anomaly. The speaker also notes bipartisan efforts involving ministers Hunt and Macfarlane and shadow ministers Bowen and Butler, and highlights that investment in large-scale renewables fell 88% in 2014.

speeches.speaker: Luke Howarth
speeches.brief: The member for Petrie supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015, which sets a large-scale renewable energy target of 33,000 gigawatt hours by 2020, increases exemptions for emissions-intensive trade-exposed activities, reinstates native forest wood waste as an eligible renewable energy source, and removes biennial reviews, while noting no changes to household solar and promoting a $20,000 instant tax write-off for small businesses.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Abbott government's changes to the Renewable Energy Target protect fossil fuel companies, undermine climate action, and harm jobs, citing 20,000 Australian jobs in renewables and $10 billion in stalled investments. They supported the target as a proven mechanism to reduce carbon emissions, contrasting it with the government's "direct action" policy, which they said cost over $600 per tonne of abatement with little benefit.

speeches.speaker: Mark Coulton
speeches.brief: The Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 was supported as restoring balance to the RET scheme by setting an achievable target, providing investment certainty, and preventing a default that would raise electricity costs. The Parkes electorate’s renewable energy projects include solar farms at Nyngan, Moree, and Lake Cargelligo, and the Bodangora wind farm.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 and its amendments, noting a capital strike in renewables over the past 18 months and citing 4,500 jobs in New South Wales’ renewables sector, as well as BlueScope Steelworks’ investment in solar-integrated Colorbond technology. They credited the members for Port Adelaide and Brand for working with the Minister to reach this point.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wilkie
speeches.brief: Opposed the Renewable Energy (Electricity) Amendment Bill 2015 for lowering the target, arguing it harms the environment and public interest; supported amendment (4) but opposed burning forest waste for energy, citing Tasmania’s experience where such practices led to widespread deforestation.

speeches.speaker: Julie Collins
speeches.brief: The speaker noted Tasmania's 86% renewable energy share and 1,500–2,000 renewable energy jobs, welcomed the RET agreement and exemption for four major industrial users (Bell Bay Aluminium, TEMCO, Nyrstar, Norske Skog), and clarified Labor's opposition to including native forest biomass in the RET while criticising the state Liberal government for sacking forestry workers.
